title: Q&A: The glassblower who repairs telescope mirrors
excerpt: Noor Haddad has spent 20 years fixing glass that astronomers can't replace.
textContent:
Noor Haddad runs a two-person glass studio outside Tucson that observatories call when a mirror or lens chips. We talked about patience, heat, and the one repair she still thinks about.

How did you end up fixing telescopes?

By accident. I was making lamps. An astronomer from the university walked in with a cracked eyepiece and said, "Nobody makes these anymore. Can you try?" I said yes before I knew what I was agreeing to.

What makes the work hard?

Glass remembers everything. If you heat one side faster than the other, it holds that stress for years and then breaks on a cold night. So the real job is cooling. Some pieces sit in the kiln for eleven days.

Is there a repair you're proudest of?

A 1910 objective lens from a small college observatory. It had a chip the size of a fingernail. I spent four months on it. When they put it back in the telescope, the first thing they looked at was Saturn, and they sent me the picture. I cried a little, honestly.

What would you tell someone starting out?

Go slower than you think you need to. The glass is never in a hurry, so you can't be either.
